title: The Many-Colored Map

pages.text: Gentle Deer found a paper-craft map that unfolded like a flower. Each petal was a different color and showed a different part of the world, with houses and foods she had never seen before.
pages.narratorLine: The world is full of people who live, eat, and celebrate in wonderfully different ways.

pages.text: Deer traced her hoof along the map. 'Why is everything so different?' she wondered. A wise old tortoise smiled. 'Different is what makes the world interesting.'
pages.narratorLine: When we look at differences with kind eyes, we see beauty instead of strangeness.

pages.text: Deer folded the map into a paper crown and wore it proudly. 'I want to learn about every petal!' she said. And Wonder World sparkled, because curiosity and kindness go hand in hand.
pages.narratorLine: Being curious about other people's lives is one of the kindest things your mind can do.

doAction.instruction: With a grown-up, learn one fact about a country or culture different from your own. Share what you learned with someone.
steps: Ask a grown-up to help you learn one interesting thing about a country you've never visited — a food, a game, or a holiday.
Tell a friend or family member the cool thing you learned.
doAction.seedlingSimplified: Ask a grown-up to tell you about a food from another country.

shinePrompt: What did you learn, and what was the most interesting part?

title: The Brave Voice Balloon

pages.text: Brave Bear saw a little paper-craft bird sitting alone at the edge of the playground. The other birds were laughing and playing, but no one had invited the little bird to join.
pages.narratorLine: Sometimes being brave doesn't mean being loud — it means speaking up for someone who feels invisible.

pages.text: Bear's heart pounded like a tiny drum. It felt scary to walk over. But he took a deep breath, and his words floated out like a bright balloon: 'Hey, would you like to play with us?'
pages.narratorLine: A brave voice starts with a kind heart that won't look away.

pages.text: The little bird's eyes went wide with surprise, then her whole face bloomed into a smile. She joined the game, and soon her laughter was the loudest of all.
pages.narratorLine: One brave invitation can change someone's whole day — and maybe even yours.

doAction.instruction: If you see someone sitting alone at school or at the park, walk over and invite them to play or sit with you.
steps: Look around at recess, in class, or at the park for someone who seems left out.
Walk up to them, smile, and say 'Would you like to play with me?' or 'Want to sit with us?'
doAction.seedlingSimplified: Say hi to someone who is sitting by themselves.

shinePrompt: How did it feel to be brave and include someone?

title: The Peaceful Pinwheel

story.title: Joyful Otter Finds Calm in the Storm

pages.text: A gust of wind blew through Wonder World and knocked over everyone's paper-craft towers. Joyful Otter and Sharing Squirrel both reached for the last standing block at the same time.
pages.narratorLine: Disagreements happen to everyone — even the best of friends.

pages.text: Their voices got louder and louder, like a storm building. Then Otter noticed a paper pinwheel spinning in the breeze. She stopped, took a deep breath, and watched it turn — slower, slower, calm.
pages.narratorLine: When you feel a storm inside, a deep breath can be like pressing pause.

pages.text: 'Let's take turns,' Otter said gently. Squirrel smiled and nodded. They rebuilt both towers together, even taller than before. The pinwheel spun happily in the peaceful breeze.
pages.narratorLine: When we solve problems with patience, we build something better than we ever could alone.

doAction.instruction: The next time you disagree with a friend or sibling, stop, take three deep breaths, and suggest taking turns instead of arguing.
steps: When you feel a disagreement starting, pause and take three slow, deep breaths.
Use a calm voice to say 'Let's take turns' or 'How can we both get what we need?'
doAction.seedlingSimplified: When you feel upset, stop and take three big breaths.

shinePrompt: Did taking a breath help you feel calmer? What happened next?

title: The Dream-Leader Crown

pages.text: The animals of Wonder World needed to build a new bridge across the river. Everyone had ideas, but nobody knew where to start. Sharing Squirrel raised her paw. 'Let's listen to every idea first.'
pages.narratorLine: A true leader doesn't just talk — they make sure everyone gets a turn to speak.

pages.text: Squirrel went around the circle. Otter suggested using logs. Deer wanted to weave vines. Bear offered to carry heavy stones. Squirrel listened to each one and found a way to use them all.
pages.narratorLine: The best plans come from many minds working together.

pages.text: By sunset, the bridge stood strong — logs for the base, vines for the rails, and stones for the path. Everyone cheered. 'We all built this!' Squirrel said, and she meant it.
pages.narratorLine: Real leaders don't take all the credit — they share the glow with everyone.

doAction.instruction: The next time you play or work with a group, ask everyone for their ideas before deciding what to do. Try to include at least one idea from each person.
steps: When your group needs to make a decision, say 'Let's hear everyone's idea first.'
Listen to each person, then suggest a plan that uses a piece of everyone's idea.
doAction.seedlingSimplified: Ask a friend 'What do you want to play?' before choosing a game.

shinePrompt: How did it feel to include everyone's ideas?

title: The Kindness Constellation

pages.text: Sweet Skunk lay on a hilltop in Wonder World, gazing at the paper-craft night sky. Each star, the old tortoise once told her, lights up when someone does something kind.
pages.narratorLine: Every act of kindness — big or small — leaves a mark that shines.

pages.text: Skunk began to count. 'Today I shared my lunch — that's one. I said sorry when I bumped into Deer — that's two. I cheered for Bear when he was scared — that's three.' The stars twinkled brighter.
pages.narratorLine: When we look back at our day, we often find more kindness than we expected.

pages.text: Soon Skunk saw a whole constellation shaped like a heart. She realized that all her small kind moments had connected into something beautiful. 'I made that,' she whispered, full of wonder.
pages.narratorLine: You are already full of kindness — sometimes you just need to stop and see it.

doAction.instruction: Before bed, sit with a grown-up and name three kind things you did today. Hold up a finger for each one, like counting stars.
steps: At bedtime, think back through your whole day.
Tell a grown-up three kind things you did — big or small — and hold up one finger for each.
doAction.seedlingSimplified: Tell a grown-up one nice thing you did today.

shinePrompt: Which of your three kind moments made you feel the proudest?
